cross_track_links.concept: reading first/last N lines of a file
cross_track_links.context: Bash uses head -n N / tail -n N. Python equivalent is open() + readlines()[:N] / [-N:], or for big files an itertools.islice approach. Bash version is a one-shot pipe-friendly tool; Python version is composable inside a larger script.

Bash idiom is `... | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n N`. Python equivalent is `collections.Counter(iterable).most_common(N)` — handles the count + sort + top-N in one call. Same gotcha applies in both: default sort/min/max on numeric strings is lexicographic in Python too (`sorted(['10','9'])` returns `['10','9']`). Convert to int before comparing.

Bash `awk '{print $11}'` and Python `line.split()[10]` both lock you to a column position. If log format shifts, both silently read the wrong word. Real-world fix in either language is regex extraction (`grep -oE` in Bash, `re.search` in Python) targeting the shape of the value (e.g. an IP), not its position.

Bash one-shot: `grep "Failed" auth.log`. Python equivalent in 4 lines: `with open(path) as f: for line in f: if "Failed" in line: print(line, end="")`. Both produce identical output for a simple substring filter. Decision factor: Bash version is pipe-friendly and ephemeral; Python version is a building block you can extend (count by IP, alert on threshold, generate report). Same task, different reuse profiles. Important shared concern: in Python, must iterate the file object directly (`for line in f:`) rather than `f.readlines()` — the latter loads the entire file into memory and crashes on production-scale logs. Bash `grep` handles arbitrary file sizes by streaming, so no equivalent gotcha exists there. This is a case where Python defaults to a footgun that Bash doesn't have.
